title: Coles Faces Bricks‑and‑Mortar Sales Decline, Downgrades Earnings Outlook
text: Coles Faces Bricks‑and‑Mortar Sales Decline, Downgrades Earnings Outlook After missing sales targets in 2024, Coles' CEO admits brick‑and‑mortar slump and outlines a new pricing strategy while online growth remains strong. The supermarket giant's adjusted half‑year earnings forecast reflects tougher competition from rivals such as Woolworths and Aldi, amidst rising inflation and shifting consumer behaviour. Coles, Australia's second‑largest grocery chain, issued a stark warning about the performance of its physical stores after the recent quarter's sales fell short of expectations, prompting a rare downgrade in its earnings forecast. The company, which operates 870 supermarkets and nearly a thousand liquor outlets under brands such as Liquorland and Vintage Cellars, recorded a 2.2 per cent rise in group sales to $11.2 billion during the 13 weeks ending September 27. While supermarkets alone contributed a 3.6 per cent increase to $10.3 billion, the figures missed market consensus and caused the stock to tumble eight per cent into the afternoon trading session.Woolworths Outperforms Rival ColesIn contrast, its chief rival Woolworths rose about 1.5 per cent to $40.60 following a stronger performance headline. CEO Leah Weckert told investors that online growth remained robust but the \"momentum\" in brick‑and‑mortar sales was disappointing. She described how shoppers are increasingly sensitive to price and more selective across a broader array of retailers, which has fragmented their baskets even as footfall in stores remains healthy.Acknowledging the headwinds of higher inflation, elevated petrol prices and rising interest rates, Weckert stressed that Coles is tightening its product mix and pricing strategy. The company is relaunching its 'Everyday Value' program-now expanded across thousands of items-and running a 'Lower Everyday Prices' initiative, offering sustained price cuts for at least six months.Financial analysts noted that the softer supermarket sales forced Coles to revise its first‑half earnings outlook from the previously anticipated increase to a flat projection of about $1.2 billion, a figure that signals caution ahead of the year's end. Despite the modest dip, the company remains committed to rebuilding customer trust in a climate of economic uncertainty.Coles Focuses On Grocery PromotionsIt plans to accelerate promotional activities, fine‑tune its messaging, and continue to keep a clear focus on the grocery promotions that now drive consumer behaviour. The move comes just as the middle of the year has seen the fastest drop in fresh produce inflation to 1.1 per cent, a decline from the 1.6 per cent rate the previous quarter, reflecting shifting cost pressures across dairy, meat and other categories.Coles' performance is mirrored by the broader sector snapshot: Woolworths reported a 4.7 per cent rise in sales to $19.4 billion for the fourteen weeks ended October 4, buoyed by a 6.9 per cent jump in supermarket sales to $14.7 billion. Coles' bottle shop unit saw a small decline of 1.3 per cent, as consumers gravitated toward smaller pack sizes and ready‑to‑drink beverages.Coles Faces Cautious Future OutlookWhile the 2025‑26 forecast for Woolworths sees a net profit of $1.1 billion up 18 per cent, Coles' projected flat result indicates a cautious stance as it works to reconcile online gains with the challenges of its physical retail footprint.
